adapter: projects: rsi6/environments/projects.py with rsi6/environments/manifests/projects.json and rsi6/data/projects/ (PSPLIB single-mode RCPSP, sets j30 and j60; 720 of the 960 instances used, the 240 of the RS = 1 classes left out). Audited in the copy at <scratch>/fresh/projects/repo. My scripts are in <scratch>/fresh/projects/audit2 (mine.py is my own parser and evaluator; check1.py to check7.py, rs.py and twins.py are the checks), and the re-fetched files are in audit2/dl.
statement: The adapter reads PSPLIB j30 and j60 correctly and evaluates the published objective exactly. I wrote my own parser, which locates each section by its title and reads rows at fixed offsets. Run on all 960 .sm files (archives read in memory), it reproduces every duration, request, capacity and precedence arc the adapter keeps. On every file the critical-path length equals the field MPM-Time and the horizon equals the sum of the durations. I also read j30opt.sm, j60hrs.sm and j60lb.sm with my own code, and the result matches the adapter on all 720 reference values and their kinds: 360 j30 optima, 282 j60 optima proven by an equal lower bound, 26 j60 values equal to the critical-path length, and 52 upper bounds. The JSON summaries agree with these values. The source publishes values only, no schedules. No valid schedule I built (5,040 of them) beats any reference. On 360 random lists in precedence order, three things agree exactly: the adapter's score(), the totals from the problem's evaluate(), and my own decoder, whose schedules I checked against every published precedence and capacity constraint. Partial evaluation is exact as well. Nothing the learner can observe changes when the stored references are altered or when training is switched between True and False, and no reference value appears in any exposed array. Relabelling permutes both activities and resources, which removes the file's topological numbering: as a list in file order it already scores 0.916 on j30 and 0.948 on j60. Malformed answers score 0. The split keeps the generation classes apart, and there are no twins across the two sides. All ten pinned hashes reproduce on disk, and the six files I fetched again reproduce them too. A reader must know three things. First, the answer form is the adapter's decision, not the benchmark's, and it does part of the scheduling: the answer is a list of activities, the serial rule turns it into a schedule, a hard group requires precedence order, and a detail group gives each candidate's finish time. Second, the zero point (the sum of the durations) compresses the scale: random lists already score 0.889 on j30, 0.930 on j60 and 0.970 on the fresh side. Third, the shipped threshold of 0.9864 is passed by the textbook latest-finish-time rule, which scores 0.9989 on the 24 fresh instances; 19 of those 24 references equal the critical-path length. A "held" verdict at this threshold is therefore not evidence of capability. The module says so itself and leaves the operating point to be set again, and that must be done before any learner answer is scored.
coverage:
CHECKED, by my own code in audit2. Total about 65 CPU-seconds, one nice'd process at a time, none over 20 s. Bytecode writing was disabled, and I confirmed that nothing under the repo changed: no file is newer than my first script and no __pycache__ appeared.
(1) Read every line of projects.py and of the manifest. No search over answers, no ordering or pruning by objective, no optimisation routine, no derived attribute. Besides parsing and evaluation, the adapter computes only two things: the forward pass earliest() (critical-path length, checked against MPM-Time, and the data-only test that leaves out instances whose earliest-start schedule fits) and the serial decoding (serial() and the fast _starts/_push). Both are kernel-side.
(2) check1.py: my parser (mine.read_sm) against the adapter's tables on all 960 files: no mismatch in d, r, R, the precedence matrix, CPL, Z, reference, kind, group or class parameters. My earliest-start test gives exactly the adapter's 240 left-out instances, which are exactly the RS = 1 classes, and on all 240 the reference equals the CPL (an independent consistency check of the solution files). Real durations lie in 1..10, no request exceeds its capacity, the numbering is topological, each of the 96 classes has one base-data file, Z - ref >= 40, NC and RF match par.sm (within 0.025 and 0.0083), and RS matches by median.
(3) check2.py: 360 valid lists on 10 instances (4 j30, 3 j60, 2 fresh, 1 upper-bound). Half were built from my parse and half from the exposed relation alone. Adapter score(), evaluate() totals [M, sum of finish times, late] and my decoder with my published-constraint validator agree 360/360. 60 brute-force checks confirmed that no earlier start fits. Of 80 lists not in precedence order, all agree: hard count equals mine, score 0. Partial evaluation: 2,346 candidate cells (positions before, at and after the next one) equal the difference of partial_totals; 792 next-position cells equal my evaluator; 30 prefixes (valid and invalid) and 708 assign steps all have totals equal to partial_totals.
(4) check3.py: observation hashes (public view fields plus a fixed script of candidates, assign, totals, evaluate and well_formed calls) on 6 instances. Unchanged by training True versus False (6/6) and by three patches of the stored value and kind (18/18). No reference equals any capacity on any of the 720 instances; durations and requests are at most 10, below every reference. 40 seeds give 40 distinct activity orders; resources are permuted; the identity in new labels is in precedence order on 0 of 72 instances; scores and totals are the same under 3 relabellings (8/8); two instances under one run seed get different relabellings. 18 degenerate answers tried.
(5) check4.py: split, halves, thresholds, layout (one over all 720), view (public fields and read-only arrays), _valid, and the test_kernel fast-evaluation check. Also the anchor's measured figures: random lists, the latest-finish-time (LFT) rule and the file order.
(6) check5.py: reference = CPL counts; greedy probes on the cost and detail groups (my own probe code, not the learner); instances where 5/5 random lists reach the reference (2 of 720); statement (2) on 80 random valid schedules that are not active (never later: 0 violations).
(7) twins.py and check6.py: no shared network, durations, requests or generator seed; all job multisets distinct; highest job-by-job similarity across classes 0.23. 100 more random-list draws on the fresh side.
(8) Manifest: sha256sum of all 10 files matches. Re-fetched j30opt.sm, j60lb.sm, j60hrs.sm, par.sm, j30.sm.tgz and library.php with the stated user agent: identical hashes. The terms quotes are verbatim on library.php; no licence or copyright statement on the library, main or download pages; the news page confirms the 06.05.2026 re-enabling of uploads.
NOT CHECKED: optimality of the references (by rule). The learner was not run (by rule), so I do not know where an untrained learner lands. run.py was read only for split, halves, layout and _valid, so how the kernel consumes threshold_for beyond these was not read. Historical claims in the module could not be checked: that 17 of 24 fresh instances were trivial before the filter, and that the 5% was fixed before any answer was scored. The module's training-side LFT figure (0.950) was not reproduced exactly: one tie draw gave 0.9454. The directories audit1, fix1 and work were not opened.
exposed:
The view exposes these fields and nothing else (checked): n_vars, n_opts, n_groups, ordered, hard, detail, capacity, var_attr, opt_attr, var_var, opt_opt, var_opt, occ_attr, domain, start_answer, start_totals, meter. Each traces as follows.
- n_vars = n_opts = J - 2 (30 or 60), from the file's 'jobs (incl. supersource/sink)'.
- var_attr: shape (n, 0), empty.
- opt_attr: shape (n, 9). Column 0 is d(j), from REQUESTS/DURATIONS 'duration'. Columns 1 to 4 are r(j,k), from 'R 1..R 4'. Columns 5 to 8 are R(k), from RESOURCEAVAILABILITIES, identical in every row. Resource order is permuted by the seed, the same way for the requests and the capacities (verified column by column against the file).
- var_var: empty.
- opt_opt[0][o,o'] = 1 when the file lists o' among the successors of o. Real jobs only: arcs from job 1 and to job J are dropped, which is exact because job 1 is the only source and job J the only sink. Permuted (verified equal to pred[perm][:, perm]).
- var_opt and occ_attr: empty.
- capacity = ones(n): each activity once, so an answer is a permutation.
- ordered = True: the positions of the list are filled in index order.
- domain, start_answer and start_totals: None.
- hard = [F, F, T] and detail = [F, T, F]. The groups are: [0] the makespan of the placed prefix, which for a complete list in precedence order is the published objective; [1] the sum of the finish times, the kernel's detail convention for a min-max objective; [2] the number of activities placed before one of their predecessors, a constraint of the answer form.
What the adapter's design hands the learner beyond the published instance:
(a) The serial rule decodes the list. It places each activity at its earliest feasible time, so lists reach only active schedules (statement (2) verified), and many lists denote the same schedule.
(b) The change of [1] tells the finish time each unplaced activity would get under the rule, which requires computing the resource profile.
(c) The change of [2] tells which activities are eligible. It also marks invalid some lists whose schedule meets every published constraint: 9 of my 80 non-precedence lists, against the module's 51 of 199.
The adapter-side object additionally holds duration, request, supply, pred, preds, succs and periods (= Z + 1). All are derived from the instance and hidden behind the view. Nothing on it is derived from a reference.
evaluator_agreement: Complete answers: 360/360 valid lists agree exactly across the adapter's score(), the problem's evaluate() totals (makespan, sum of finish times, late count = 0) and my independent serial decoder with my own validator of the published constraints. The score is (Z - M)/(Z - ref) with my own Z and my own parsed reference; it is identical as a float. 60 brute-force checks confirmed the rule takes the smallest feasible start. 80/80 lists not in precedence order agree: the hard count equals mine and the score is 0. Partial evaluation: 2,346/2,346 candidate cells equal the difference of partial_totals (positions before, at and after the next one; rows of used options are zero); 792/792 next-position cells equal my evaluator; for 30/30 prefixes, totals() equals partial_totals() equals mine; 708 assign steps all consistent. References: my own table reader of j30opt.sm, j60hrs.sm and j60lb.sm equals env.reference() on all 720 instances, and my classification equals env.reference_kind() on all 720. The JSON summaries agree with the text files. The source publishes no reference answers (values only), so none could be scored. As substitute checks: the reference equals the CPL on all 240 left-out instances; no reference is below the CPL; and none of 5,040 valid schedules I built (random, LFT and file order) has a makespan below any reference.

findings.title: Shipped threshold is passed by a one-pass textbook rule on the fresh split, so 'held' says nothing here
findings.problem: The threshold is the mean score of makespans 5% above the reference: 0.9864 on the kernel's 24 fresh instances (halves 0.9876 and 0.9840). The latest-finish-time (LFT) rule passes it easily. The rule uses only exposed arrays (one backward pass over the durations and the successor relation) and its list is decoded by the same serial rule. It scores 0.9989 on the fresh instances (0.9982 to 0.9996 over tie draws) and 0.9998 and 0.9986 on the two halves. The fresh side is three j60 classes with RS 0.5 and 0.7, and on 19 of its 24 instances the reference equals the critical-path length; this holds on 7 of 16 training instances and 273 of 720 overall. So the fresh side mostly asks for a schedule as long as the critical path, which is what LFT targets. The module admits the problem (lines 178-180): a mean score at the threshold is 'not by itself a capability beyond this one-pass rule; an operating point above it would have to be fixed again, before any answer of a learner is scored here (this adapter does not do that)'. As shipped, the kernel counts as 'held' a level that a textbook rule reaches. Random lists (0.970) and greedy use of the exposed evaluator (0.965 to 0.971) do not reach it, so the threshold separates only those from LFT. The anchor text itself is accurate.
findings.evidence: cd audit2 && PYTHONPATH=repo OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 nice -n 10 python3 -I check4.py printed: 'threshold attr 0.9864 env.threshold 0.986418 | ... halves 0.9876 0.984'; 'LFT on fresh: mean 0.9989 min 0.9982 max 0.9996 | halves: 0.9998 0.9986'; 'random lists on fresh: mean 0.9703 ... draws >= threshold: 0 of 60'. check5.py printed: 'fresh: ref == CPL on 19 of 24; upper bounds 1 [j6043_4]', 'train: ref == CPL on 7 of 16', 'all used: ref == CPL on 273 of 720', 'greedy on the cost group [0] ... fresh [0.9689 0.9709 0.9708]', 'greedy on the detail group [1] ... fresh [0.9705 0.9669 0.965]'. check6.py printed: '100 draws ... mean 0.9704 sd 0.0037 min 0.9603 max 0.9779; >= threshold: 0'.
findings.fix: Before any learner answer is scored on this category, define threshold_for(ids) relative to the rule the module already measures: the mean score, on exactly those instances, of the LFT list (latest finish times by one backward pass from the critical-path length over durations and the successor relation; ties broken by a fixed seed written in the module), decoded by serial(). Then 'held' means at least what the textbook rule does. Pin its value on the kernel's fresh split (about 0.9989) in threshold, and rewrite anchor to say this. Add that the fresh split leaves only about 0.001 of headroom above the rule, because 19 of the 24 references equal the critical-path length. If that bar is judged unusable, keep 0.9864 but make anchor and every report on this category state that 'held' here is reached by the one-pass LFT rule, and report the LFT score next to the learner's.

findings.title: Score scale compressed at the top: gains on this category look small next to other categories
findings.problem: The zero point Z (the sum of the durations) is exact, closed-form and correct: every list in precedence order has M <= Z, the score is monotone in the makespan, and the arithmetic is exact. But it lies far below what valid lists do. Random lists in precedence order already score 0.889 on j30, 0.930 on j60 and 0.970 on the fresh split, and 0.01 of score equals 1.83% of makespan on j30 and 3.21% on j60. A capability that shortens j60 makespans by 6% shows up as a gain of about 0.02. Gains or m_net compared or averaged with categories whose zero point is a chance value (genassign, for example) will understate this category. The module text discloses the compression; the anchor and the scores do not carry it.
findings.evidence: check4.py printed: 'j30 0.01 of score = mean 1.83 % of makespan', 'j60 0.01 of score = mean 3.21 % of makespan', 'j30 ... random 0.8890 (makespan 17.0% above ref)', 'j60 ... random 0.9296 (makespan 19.4% above ref)', 'random lists on fresh: mean 0.9703'.
findings.fix: Keep Z. Report with every score on this category the mean makespan excess (M/ref - 1) of the same answers (kernel side, from score's own schedule), and state in anchor the random-list baseline on the fresh split (0.970) and the conversion (0.01 of score is about 3.2% of j60 makespan). Before comparing or aggregating gains across categories, divide them by (1 - random-list baseline).
